procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court (convicted and sentenced the accused under Sections 302, 307, and 324 IPC)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 17.08.2012 passed by the Division Bench of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Hyderabad in Criminal Appeal No. I 025 of 2008.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused, being aggrieved by the Trial Court's decision, appealed to the High Court of Andhra Pradesh. The High Court allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence imposed by the Trial Court, and acquitted the accused.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Complainant, being aggrieved by the High Court's decision, appealed to the Supreme Court by way of special leave. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order passed by the High Court, affirming the order passed by the trial Court.

directions: The concerned Police Authorities to take custody of the respondent forthwith to serve out the remainder of sentence imposed by the Trial Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in failing to appreciate the evidence and setting aside the well-reasoned order of the trial court without giving any reasons, rendering its decision perverse and unsustainable.

facts: The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence that was before the High Court, including the testimony of injured eyewitnesses (PWs 1 and 2), witnesses who arrived at the scene shortly after the incident (PWs 20-22), and other evidence such as the FSL report, the weapon used, and the sketch of the crime scene.
The Supreme Court noted that the trial court had issued a "well reasoned order" based on this evidence.
The High Court, in contrast, set aside the trial court's order.
The High Court also set aside a conviction under Section 307 without specifically overturning the trial court's reasoning and findings on that charge.
law: An appellate court (the High Court) cannot set aside a well-reasoned order of a lower court (the trial court) without providing plausible reasons.
A judicial decision is considered "perverse" and "not sustainable in the eyes of law" if it fails to appreciate or consider the material evidence on record.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had failed to appreciate the evidence presented, particularly the compelling testimony from injured eyewitnesses (PWs 1 and 2) and other witnesses (PWs 20-22).

The Court determined that the High Court had not given any plausible reasons for its decision, other than a single point regarding motive, which was insufficient to overturn the trial court's comprehensive judgment.
The Supreme Court characterized the High Court's judgment as a "non-reasoned order" for its failure to engage with the evidence and the trial court's findings.
This failure to consider the evidence and provide adequate reasoning led the Supreme Court to deem the High Court's decision "perverse on all counts."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, concluding that the High Court erred by failing to appreciate the evidence and by setting aside the trial court's well-reasoned order without giving sufficient reasons. Consequently, the Supreme Court found the High Court's order to be perverse and unsustainable, set it aside, and affirmed the order of the trial court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court's decision to set aside the conviction under Section 307 was erroneous, especially when it had not set aside the trial court's finding and reasoning that the offence was made out.

facts: The trial court convicted the accused for offences including one under Section 307 IPC (attempt to murder).
On appeal, the High Court acquitted the accused of all charges, setting aside the conviction under Section 307.

The Supreme Court observed that the High Court overturned the conviction under Section 307 without specifically setting aside the trial court's findings and reasoning which had established that the offence was made out.
law: An appellate court cannot set aside a conviction without first addressing and setting aside the specific findings and reasoning of the trial court that led to that conviction.
A judgment that fails to appreciate evidence and overturns a well-reasoned order without providing sufficient reasons of its own is considered perverse and not sustainable in law.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court committed a significant error by setting aside the conviction under Section 307 while leaving the trial court's foundational reasoning and findings of fact intact.
The Court noted this was part of a broader failure by the High Court to properly appreciate the evidence, such as ignoring the "dying declaration" made by the victim of the attempted murder (PW-2).
The Supreme Court characterized the High Court's order as a "non-reasoned order" that improperly overturned the "well reasoned order of the Trial Court."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's decision to set aside the conviction under Section 307 was erroneous and perverse. It held that the High Court could not simply ignore the trial court's findings that the offence was made out. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order of acquittal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in failing to appreciate the evidence and setting aside the well-reasoned order of the trial court without giving any reasons, rendering its decision perverse and unsustainable.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred in acquitting the accused without taking into consideration the well-reasoned judgment of the Trial Court and completely ignoring the evidence of P.Ws 1 and 2, who were eyewitnesses and injured witnesses.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's counsel cited judgments in support of their case, which the Supreme Court found unhelpful in the given facts and circumstances.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court's decision to set aside the conviction under Section 307 was erroneous, especially when it had not set aside the trial court's finding and reasoning that the offence was made out.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred in setting aside the conviction (which included the offence under Section 307) by ignoring the well-reasoned judgment of the trial court and the evidence of eyewitnesses.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's counsel cited judgments to support the High Court's decision to acquit the accused of all charges, including the one under Section 307.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An appellate court's order is perverse and legally unsustainable if it sets aside a well-reasoned order of a trial court without appreciating the evidence on record and without providing sufficient reasons for its decision.
obiter: A High Court's order is flawed when it sets aside a conviction under a specific section of the law without first setting aside the trial court's finding and reasoning that the offence under that section was made out.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's decision to acquit the accused is perverse and legally unsustainable. It erroneously set aside the trial court's well-reasoned conviction order without providing any plausible reasons of its own, aside from an insufficient finding on motive. The High Court completely failed to appreciate crucial evidence, including the credible testimony of two injured eyewitnesses, and illogically overturned the conviction under Section 307 without refuting the trial court's specific findings that established the offence.
legal_tests_applied: The 'perversity' standard of appellate review, under which a higher court's judgment is deemed perverse and unsustainable if it sets aside a well-reasoned lower court order without providing its own plausible reasons, fails to appreciate material evidence on record, or reaches a conclusion that is illogical and contrary to the evidence.
why_respondent_won: The High Court set aside the trial court's well-reasoned order without giving any plausible reasons of its own, with the sole exception of motive, which was insufficient to justify the acquittal.
The High Court failed to appreciate the evidence brought before it, particularly the credible testimony of the injured eyewitnesses, PWs 1 and 2.

The High Court's order was illogical because it set aside the conviction under Section 307 without first setting aside the trial court's specific finding and reasoning that the offence had been made out based on the evidence.
policy_considerations: An appellate court has a duty to provide a reasoned judgment when overturning a trial court's conviction. It cannot simply ignore the trial court's detailed analysis and the evidence on record, as doing so undermines the integrity of the judicial process.
